newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Dec 29.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Dec 29.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
SUNDAY TELEGRAPH
-- HANSON SET FOR BIG US SHAKE-UP

Hanson is planning a shake-up of its American construction operations once its demerger is completed in February. This could see the sale or demerger of Spectrum, the contracting subsidiary that had sales of 600 million pounds stg last year. The group is also considering buying a massive one-off insurance policy to cover its environmental liabilities.
-- ENERGY GROUP RAISES 1.1 BILLION POUND WAR CHEST

The Energy Group, the electricity and coal mining group demerged from Hanson has raised an acquisition fund of almost 1.1 billion pounds stg in a deal with its banks. It has sold them a revenue stream from the power stations acquired from the generating companies in exchange for a cash payment of 1,097 million pounds, radically reducing its debts.
-- JARDINE STAFF BARRED FROM PERSONAL DEALS

In a move to restore its reputation, Jardine Fleming, the Far Eastern arm of Robert Fleming, has banned all personal share dealing by fund managers. Sources say the deal could soon be imitated throughout Hong Kong, but is likely to be resisted in London.
-- FLEMING SEEKS NEW CITY HOME

Robert Fleming is looking for new City of London offices for its trading operations. It needs to double its space by 2000AD. It joins a growing list of banks and brokers who have boosted the London property market with their shift plans.
-- MORGAN PROBE COST HITS 2 MILLION POUNDS

Fund management regulator IMRO has spent two million pounds stg investigating Morgan Grenfell Asset Management and rogue fund manager Peter Young. The regulator is to demand Morgan pay the amount in full.
SUNDAY TIMES
-- FAYEDS PUT TELEVISION ON THEIR SHOPPING LIST

The Fayed brothers, owners of Harrods, are set to move into television, building on their media interests through Liberty Publishing. The possibility of launching a shopping channel enabling consumers from around the country to sample the luxury goods on offer in the world's most famous department store, is being discussed.
-- BRANSON IS MOST ADMIRED BUSINESSMAN

Richard Branson is Britain's best known businessman as well as the most popular, according to a Sunday Times poll. The poll also demonstrates how little an impression most business leaders have made on the British public despite 17 years of Tory rule dedicated to reviving popular capitalism.
-- JOB PROSPECTS AT SEVEN-YEAR HIGH FOR 1997

According to the latest Sunday Times/Manpower WorkWatch survey, job prospects in Britain are at a seven-year high going into 1997. The survey shows that the manufacturing sector is the most optimistic.
-- CITY FORECASTS 5 PER CENT RISE IN SHARE PRICES NEXT YEAR

Top market strategists in the City have predicted a steady ride for the London stock market in 1997, with the average forecast seeing the FT-SE 100 index rising around 5.5 per cent. There is a wide spread of forecasts with strategists placing a different emphasis on the effects of the general election and likely increases in interest rates.
-- BT IN MILLENNIUM PROTEST

British Telecom who are one of the top private-sector sponsors of the millennium celebrations based around Greenwich has protested to the government over delays and general inefficiency in organising the project. It has expressed concern over the departure of Barry Hartop as chief executive of Millennium Central, who will administer the celebration.
THE OBSERVER
-- CRASH SCOTCHES WHISKY SCHEMES

Securitized Syndicated Investments, trading as Marshall Wineries, one of the biggest companies selling malt whisky went into voluntary liquidation on 12 December with debts of more than 700,000 pounds stg and assets of only 33,000 pounds stg.
-- HOUSE PRICES RISE ECHOES EIGHTIES

Figures published by the Halifax Building Society this week show that house prices went up by between seven and eight per cent, the first substantial annual increase since the 1980s. There is now general agreement that house prices will rise between seven and eight per cent in 1997.
-- BACK TO WORK FOR 100 POUNDS A WEEK

A new study of life at the bottom of Britain's 'hire and fire' labour market shows that people moving off benefits into work typically earn just 100 pounds stg a week, less than half the average wage for all jobs and some 12 per cent less in real terms than the equivalent figure in 1980.
-- LABOUR FACES EARLY PRESSURE TO COME CLEAN

Senior Whitehall sources say that a new Labour government will almost immediately be forced to set out its position on key international economic issues. A Blair administration would have to set out a considered UK view first at the European Council in Amsterdam 16-17 June and than at the World Economic Summit in Denver, Colorado, later the same week.
-- ANOTHER 48 HOURS FOR SOCIETY SAVERS

Savers with the Halifax, Woolwich Building Society, Bristol & West Building Society and Northern Rock building societies, all converting next year, have just two days to make sure that they have at least 100 pounds stg in one or more share accounts to qualify for free minimum share or cash bonuses.
INDEPENDENT ON SUNDAY
-- POST OFFICE MAKES BID FOR FREEDOM

Following a record Christmas for Royal Mail deliveries, the Post Office is lobbying the government and the Labour Party for more freedom to compete with the private sector. In 1997, it hopes to move into household and other personal insurance, as well as opening a full travel agency service.
-- HOLIDAY SALES AT RECORD LEVELS

Record numbers of Britons have booked their summer holidays early, prompted, according to travel agents, by a return of the 'feelgood factor'. Sales for 1997 are already up by 30 per cent, to a record 2.3 million, with the trend expected to continue through January.
-- BID WATCHDOG UNDER FIRE

The Takeover Panel was attacked this weekend by top investment institutions for denying them the chance for a better price in CalEnergy's 780 million pounds stg hostile bid for Northern Electric. Investors are critical of the Panel's inconsistency in overruling its executive and extending the bid's closing date for four days until Christmas Eve.
-- BIG SPENDERS OUT IN FORCE FOR SALES

Above average consumer spending in the Christmas sales is thought by city Analysts, to have rescued retailers from an indifferent pre-Christmas shopping period. Spending in the sales is expected to bring figures back into line with earlier predictions of sales growth in December of about seven percent over the same month last year.
-- UK ECONOMY TO LEAD THE WAY IN EUROPE

The UK economy will be the top performer among European economies in 1997 according to City economists. Investors are also thought to be relaxed about the outcome of the general election believing that whoever wins will continue on a similar track, and lead to a further year of progress.
MAIL ON SUNDAY
-- TITAN REVIVAL BID BACKED BY TREASURY 'WISE MEN'

Professor Patrick Minford, a top adviser to the Treasury, is backing the revival of a get-rich-quick scheme condemned six years ago. He wants the government to overturn the ban on the Titan scheme, calling the pyramid-type scheme a 'legitimate gamble'.
-- LEADING BROKER TO QUIT LLOYD'S

Leading insurance broker FMW Insurance is pulling out of Lloyd's. The broker faces rising costs to stay in the market, but places only a fraction of its business there. It is the first defection of a top broker since the market restructured.
-- BT MAY MARKET ELECTRICITY AND GAS

British Telecom may market electricity and gas through a link-up with a power company. The company has already been in talks with United Utilities and others. The move may start a trend of partnerships between utilities and other operations.
-- AIRBUS JOBS ARE SET FOR TAKE OFF

The UK is the likely location for the construction of a factory to build the jets planned by the four-nation Airbus partnership. Three of the six sites being considered are owned by British Aerospace. The others are in France and Germany.
-- 18 MILLION POUND GRAVY TRAIN ON ROADS

Labour have attacked the government for spending 18 million pounds stg on privately financed road projects' administration and consultants. A leaked Department of Transport document also reveals interest and VAT have made Private Finance Initiative roads more expensive than conventionally-funded projects.
